utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. May the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. May we have we appearances, please, starting with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, and counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Deputy Prosecutor, David Tolbert; myself, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon much, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my colleagues on the Prosecution, everybody in the courtroom. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. Nicholas Robson, and I represent the Defence of Mr. Rasim Delic, together will our case manager, Ms. Lana Deljkic, and our legal assistants, Ms. Lejla Gluhic and Asja Zujo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we start the proceedings of the day, I just wanted to raise one little point, which relates to an earlier decision that the Court made. We're going to render an oral decision in this respect. The Trial Chamber now stands to address a matter in relation to the Law Library documents. On the 15th of June, 2007, the Trial Chamber issued a decision admitting into evidence the 48 so-called Law Library documents which had been jointly tendered by the parties. In the decision, the Trial Chamber also ordered the Registrar to assign one exhibit number to this collection of documents on the first day of the presentation of evidence of the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber has been informed by the Registry that due to technical limitations of the e-court system, it is not feasible to keep such a large collection of documents under one exhibit number. The Trial Chamber also notes that an amended index of the documents was provided to the Trial Chamber by the parties, together with the Law Library documents on the 1st of June, 2007. In a letter from the Prosecution to the Trial Chamber attached to this amended index and the documents, the Prosecution stated that two documents have not been assigned ERN numbers and that it will notify the Trial Chamber of ERN numbers once they are assigned. In the letter, the Prosecution also noted that part or parts of the document PT-40-37 have yet to be translated into English. This is also mentioned in the index. The Trial Chamber orders, one, the Registrar to assign individual consecutive exhibit to the 48 documents; two, the parties to provide the missing English translation, unless this has already been done, by the 13th of July, 2007; three, the parties to amend the index of the documents in light of the above and to include references to the respective documents' exhibit number; four, the index be admitted into evidence as the first exhibit in the consecutive series of exhibit numbers. Thank you very much. After that, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We will certainly, Your Honours, ensure that that is provided no later than the 13th of July, 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Prosecution is grateful for the pre-trial decisions that were rendered earlier this morning. However, in light of the decision concerning the reconsideration with respect to the amount of time and number of witnesses afforded to the Prosecution, the Prosecution, at this point in time, Your Honours, is not ready to proceed. We would, however, ask for a few days in order to assimilate the decisions that were rendered earlier this morning and perhaps to be afforded an opportunity to further explain to the Trial Chamber why the amount of time that has been made available to us and the number of witnesses which have been afforded the Prosecution needs to be increased. And we would ask for an opportunity to present further arguments on that issue, in light of the decisions which were just rendered this morning, including the decision rejecting the Prosecution motion for a reconsideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you done?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How much time are you asking for?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. Madam Vidovic, Judge Harhoff wanted to ask a question to counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I apologise for taking the floor. I just wanted to clarify from Mr. Mundis. What are you seeking, a couple of extra days, in order to consider these matters, or how am I to understand your application?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would suggest it depends in part on whether these further submissions would be done in writing or orally. I would believe that we would be in a position perhaps in three days' time to orally address the Trial Chamber on all of these issues, including, if it would be helpful, a more detailed explanation as to why the Prosecution submits that we would require approximately 70 witnesses and slightly more than 100 hours of direct examination time in order to prove our case. If the Trial Chamber would be inclined to have those submissions in writing, that might take a few additional days in order to prepare written submissions on that point. We would certainly be in a position to do that by one week from today, if it were to be in writing, or perhaps Thursday of this week if it were to be done orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our position is as follows: We are ready to proceed to trial, and we leave the Prosecution motion to the Trial Chamber for its ultimate decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have a question to you then, Mr. Mundis, now that the Defence leaves it to the Chamber. What you do you need to tell the Chamber in three days or so? Are you not able to tell the Chamber now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Prosecutor's position, we believe, has been made clear both in our written submission of Friday of last week, as well as the submissions that were made during the Rule 11 bis referral hearing on Friday afternoon. Our position, in a nutshell, is it's not possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? You are aware that this Chamber is not seized of the Referral, the 11 bis motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I am certainly aware of that, Your Honours. But in the event that any or all of the Chamber had read the transcripts of that, that's why I made reference to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. If not, we can certainly, in a nutshell, indicate, once again, our position is that it is simply not -- we are not in a position to be able to prove our case with 55 witnesses and a cumulative total of 170 hours, to include cross-examination, redirect, questions from the Bench, and procedural matters, in addition to direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, Mr. Mundis, I guess you have read this afternoon's decision by the Chamber, and you'll also be aware of the provisions of Rule 73 bis (F). Are you not inclined to make use of that, which you can do now, immediately at the start of the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position is that we need to have a higher degree of certainty with respect to the amount of time and number of witnesses available to us, and I don't mean to be flippant or curt. But our position is if we are required to start the trial under these conditions, the likely outcome would be an acquittal. We cannot risk the possibility that the Trial Chamber, whether it's five minutes after I open or five days after I open or five weeks after I open, we cannot run the risk that the Trial Chamber would deny that motion for additional time or additional witnesses. And to start a trial -- I need to be very clear. To start a trial, when this office believes there is insufficient time or witnesses to prove the charges, is irresponsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, I -- excuse me, I'm trying to follow the logic of your argument. You feel you cannot come back to this Chamber by way of a Rule 73 bis (F) motion because you cannot risk a denial. You, in the same breath, want a postponement for three days to allow you to come back to say exactly what I'm asking you to say in the 73 bis motion, and you have the belief that you can persuade us when you come back in three days' time. Why can't you just put that argument, Mr. Mundis, in terms of the Rules of this Tribunal on a 73 bis (F) motion, and we can reconsider your motion? What is just so difficult? And then we can start the trial in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, can I just add, on behalf of the Chamber and just in continuation of what the President has just told you, that, of course, the Chamber is in no way seeking to interfere or make the life of the Prosecution more difficult than necessary. The decision that we took to cut down the number of witnesses and the number of hours for the Prosecution to present its case was based on all the material that we had seen and, genuinely, what we thought would be sufficient for you to prove the case. And we also had in mind that since there are, in effect, only basically two counts to prove, we thought, genuinely and honestly, that 55 witnesses and 170 hours would be sufficient. We see that the major challenge in this trial is the fact that the accused is among the highest-ranking persons, and that, as you said also in your interventions during the 11 bis hearing, that was something that makes this case more difficult than it, otherwise, would have been if it had just been a 7.1 bis case. But we took that into account as well. In fact, the only argument that we've heard so far for you to explain to us why you think that it is impossible for you to make your case with the 55 witnesses and the 170 hours is the fact that it is a 73 case. Well, when we look at the list of witnesses which you had proposed, it seemed to us that most of the witnesses that you intended to bring and testify before us were witnesses who could testify to the crimes on the ground, and we saw not many witnesses who would be able to bring important and relevant evidence about the link that would link the events on the ground up to the level of the accused. And this is why we thought that, as much as it is important to hear the testimonies of the victims, we also have to put the right dimensions to this case, and, again, that is why we reached the number. Then, when you made these very violent and vociferous operations, we then thought, well, we're open to discussion. We're are ready to hear you out. But so far, I must say, that the Chamber has heard nothing that can substantiate why you think it is impossible for you to make your case with this limited number. And if you have additional reasons or arguments that we have not heard yet or which were one of the other reasons you can't bring to us in public session, then let's move to another forum, but at least explain to us what the problem is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Harhoff. Let me just be as brief as I can, under the situation. First of all, the Prosecution does not necessarily agree that the majority of the witnesses go to the crime base in this case. In fact, I believe fewer than -- or approximately, fewer than one-third of the actual total of witnesses actually are what might be considered crime-based witnesses. And, certainly, with respect to the Maline incident, there's only a very small number of witnesses, perhaps five or six, that are considered to be crime-based witnesses. The bulk of the witnesses are security-type people, inside-type witnesses, witnesses who will testify as to issues concerning command and control, issues concerning the presence of the Mujahedin or foreign fighters in units of the ARBiH, and we would not agree that a large number of witnesses in this case are crime-based witnesses. And if our 65 ter summaries gave that impression, then perhaps we need to relook at that issue. What I am suggesting, and perhaps a Rule 65 ter hearing might be more appropriate or a status conference might be a more appropriate forum for this, is the Prosecution is prepared to go down the entire list of witnesses and briefly explain to the Trial Chamber the purpose of their testimony and to distinguish that testimony from other witnesses for whom the Trial Chamber might think that evidence is cumulative. And to undertake that exercise, in light of the Chamber's earlier rulings this morning concerning Rule 94(B) and concerning adjudicated facts, we would be in a position to clearly articulate why we need approximately 70 witnesses in order to prove our case. And what I'm simply saying, to answer the Presiding Judge's question, is that that is not something that we are in a position to do today, but I believe we would be in a position to do orally three days from now or in detailed written pleadings one week from today. To briefly answer the Presiding Judge's other question about Rule 73 bis (F), I would simply submit that that provision is one which is designed primarily for those situations where, having invoked Rule 73 bis (C), sometime much later in the proceedings, the Prosecution would come back and say, it's now clear, it's now clear, six or seven or eight weeks or six or seven or eight months into the trial, that we need more time or more witnesses. I'm not asking for relief under Rule 73 bis (F) at this stage because the trial has not commenced. So what we're asking the Trial Chamber to do is to exercise its inherent discretion to reconsider its decisions or any decision that the Trial Chamber has the inherent discretion to reconsider. And we're asking for that reconsideration before the trial so that both the Prosecution and perhaps even more importantly the Defence knows exactly which witnesses will be called at trial. And it's that issue which is why we have brought this matter to the attention of the Trial Chamber before the case starts. So I clearly understand that Rule 73 bis (F) can be invoked by the parties after the case. We're not asking for that, because our position is we need to know before the case starts so that we can plan in the most expeditious way to move this case forward. And, again, I would assert that it's for the benefit of the Defence as well, so that they don't operate under the assumption that we're going to be calling 55 witnesses, where I know full well that I will be forced to make that 73 bis (F) motion very shortly into the trial in order to be in a position to prove my case. And, again, as I indicated at the beginning, it would be irresponsible for me to commence a trial knowing that if that decision cannot altered, the accused will be acquitted. That would not be the best use of the resources of this institution, with all due respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, while you say that -- you tell us the purpose of Rule 73 bis (F), I don't see that purpose in the reading of the Rule. The reading of the Rule says once the trial has commenced, you can use that Rule to apply to increase. That's the first point, and let me just carry on a little bit. Now, this Trial Chamber made a decision on the 2nd of July setting the number of witnesses that the Prosecution may call and the number of hours that may be used by the Prosecution. The Prosecution asked for a reconsideration. Now, again, a decision has been given on that motion for reconsideration, and the reason for the decision that is given is that the motion for reconsideration is not motivated. And I'm sure if you re-read that motion, you will see that it is not motivated. You are asking us to reconsider and use our inherent discretion to reconsider a motion when we don't have arguments before us for reconsideration. Now, I'm saying, or at least the Chamber is trying to say to you, we are prepared to give the Prosecution an opportunity to give a reasoned argument for reconsideration, be it 73 bis (F), be it whatever manner you want to do it, by all means. And this Trial Chamber will look favorably to any reasoned presentation and well-motivated presentation. But we cannot afford to delay the start of the trial because of all manner of reasons that you can imagine; the fairness to the accused, the need to be as expeditious as we possibly can be with the running of trials. And there is nothing, I can see absolutely nothing, stopping the Prosecution from beginning now with the trial; and either, in three days' time, come with an oral motion to motivate or, in a week's time, come with a written application or written motion for reconsideration, a well-motivated motion. We agree with you. The only problem is we need to start. And I don't see why -- I can't see the reason for the Prosecution not wanting to start simply because of what you are saying, because once you have put your case before the Chamber and we have reconsidered that, the Chamber will give a decision according to how it sees the facts, and the list of witnesses may be changed. It's early in the trial now for that to be prejudicial to the Defence, I would imagine. They know the number of witnesses that the Prosecution is about to call in the next week or so, and this motion can be dealt with in a week's time, Mr. Mundis, if you just begin with the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it is precisely for the reason that we would like to have the opportunity of a few days' time to put together these very arguments that it would seem the Trial Chamber is eager to hear. Our position, however, partially because Your Honour just stressed, that the Trial Chamber may, may, give us the relief we're seeking, that's the problem, in the sense that I cannot start -- I cannot risk starting the trial without the certainty of knowing which witnesses I'm going to be allowed to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So I hear you now. I understand what you're saying. You're putting a gun to the head of the Chamber. You're saying, "You've got to guarantee me that you're going to grant my motion; otherwise, I'm not starting." Is that how I understand you, because it is always "may," Mr. Mundis, it always depends on the arguments put forward. If you make a case, you get a positive answer. If you don't make a case, you don't get a positive answer. You can't expect this Trial Chamber, at this stage, to guarantee you that it shall. It can only say it may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, with all due respect, that is the very decision that the Office of the Prosecutor needs to have, not whether it will be given the more time, but we need to know, having been afforded the opportunity to fully brief the Chamber on the issue and to fully explain it, if our arguments at that point are unpersuasive, then we will take whatever steps the Office of the Prosecutor feels need to be taken. If I could just finish, if the decision of the Trial Chamber, as it stands now, remains the same a week from now, after we make those further submissions, then this Office will take the position that it feels needs to be taken under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And so the point is, simply, if we can be given the opportunity to be heard on this point before the trial starts, so that we know absolutely certainly, having made full submissions, that the Chamber's position remains the same, that we have 55 witnesses and 170 hours total, then we will take the steps necessary. But we would certainly, at this point, simply ask for the delay of a few days, which in our respectful submission is not extremely prejudicial to the Defence. It's simply so that the Chamber has all the information it needs in order to possibly reconsider its decision. And if we're unsuccessful, then we will take the steps needed at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, all that you are asking for is not being denied -- is not being disputed. The Chamber is prepared to give you those few days. What I do not understand is the link between the start of the trial and the rendering of the decision on what you want to put before the Court. I can't see why we can't start. We can start now, you can have as much time as you need and collect your thoughts, put your motion on paper, bring it orally. We will listen to it, and we will give you a decision accordingly. Now, you are not telling me why we cannot now start the trial, sir. And I think we now are debating this thing and going in circles, and I think we've got to come down to resolving this issue, you know. At least we've got to start. You can give your opening statements, and we can have a 65 ter meeting tomorrow. We can have a 65 ter meeting as and when you think you are ready to have it, but we can be starting the case. You haven't given me the link between these two, and I'm saying to you, this is precious time. I wouldn't like to waste this precious time. I would like to make use of today to hear opening statements, and then you can come later with everything you want to come with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I just have a moment to consult, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The short answer to the question as to why we are not in a position to proceed today is actually quite simple. Until we know the exact size of our case and the amount of time available to us, and have had time to digest the pre-trial rulings that were rendered this morning, I am not in a position to fully articulate the scope of that case. In other words, I'm not sure if I'm going to be opening about this part of the case or that part of the case until I know which witnesses I'm calling and the full scope of what I'm to be dealing with. I understand that that might be not fully satisfactory; but the truth of the matter is, I don't know if I'm calling 55 witnesses or if somewhere down the road I might have more witnesses than that, and the full scope of my case cannot be presented with 55 witnesses. So by definition, I cannot start explaining a case when I, myself, don't know the full scope of the case I'm going to be allowed to put before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: With respect, indeed, you are right, Mr. Mundis, that is not persuasive indeed. I don't think that explaining, in an opening statement, the scope of your case has to do with the number of witnesses you are going to call. This Trial Chamber is aware, everybody is aware, everybody can hear you, that you want more witnesses. All you're doing in an opening statement is giving us the scope of your case as fully as you know it to be. And you know you are going to either put further arguments before the Trial Chamber for more witnesses and more hours. And if I may address the question that you raised a little earlier, if, at that time, you still get a negative answer, I don't see what stops the Prosecution from taking the decision it would have taken had it known in advance that they are not getting more witnesses and more time. At that time, you can still take that decision, sir. So I don't see why we cannot start now, Mr. Mundis. Let's start the case, because there is no link between the start and the resolution of the motion for more witnesses and more time. That motion, if well motivated, it will be considered. If not -- and that's why at this stage the only answer that the Chamber can say is, yes, it may grant the motion, but it can't give a guarantee without having seen the papers. We've got to see the papers, we've got to hear the argument, we've got to hear what the Defence has to say, we've got to weigh arguments, and then give a decision. So, yes, the answer is "may," but having given that answer, whatever the answer, positive or negative, the Prosecution -- it's still open to the Prosecution to take the decisions it wants to take and to take the actions it wants to take. There is no bar to starting today. Can we start with the opening statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would respectfully request a brief adjournment. I need to take further instructions on this matter from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. How long for you to consider?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Twenty minutes. Court adjourns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, once again. Apologies for taking much longer than the 20 minutes that we said we were going to take. Factors beyond our control kept us out. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Before the Prosecution commences with its opening, I would like to take this opportunity to introduce to the Trial Chamber the Prosecution trial team for this case, the faces that you'll be seeing. To my immediate right is Laurie Sartorio; next to her is Kyle Wood; and, finally, Aditya Menon. One other member of the team, Matthias Neuner, is currently assigned to another case and is unable to be with us this afternoon, but will be appearing for the Prosecution throughout these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are all defined by the values which we cherish. We are all judged by the decisions we make in defending those values. There is much truth in the old saying "actions speak louder than words." Inaction, however, especially in the face of an obligation to act, speaks even louder. In short, this is a case about values, decisions, and inaction. As a man of arms, the values which the accused, Rasim Delic, fought for were noble. The decisions which he took in defending those values are the foundation of the charges which he must now answer before this International Tribunal. The Prosecution has alleged that as the Supreme Commander of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the accused, Rasim Delic, failed in his duty to prevent certain crimes from being carried out by his units over which he exercised effective control. Alternatively, the Prosecution has alleged that the accused, as the Supreme Commander of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina throughout the indictment period, failed with respect to his obligations to punish the perpetrators of those crimes, having been put on notice that such crimes had been committed. These failures, this inaction, if you will, is what this case is all about. Thus, the case, from a conceptual point of view, is actually quite simple. He had a duty to act, he failed in that duty; and as a result, crimes were committed and perpetrators were allowed to escape justice. On another level, however, the case is complex. As a so-called 7.3-only case, many aspects must be established through circumstantial evidence. Many aspects must be established through large numbers of documents, which will require witnesses who will come in and explain the context in which those documents were created. Other aspects of the case, such as the failure to punish, will require the proof of a negative; that is, that no one was prosecuted, no one was investigated, no one was charged, no one was convicted. For these reasons, in this opening that you're hearing today, the Prosecution has opted to rely mainly on a number of documents and maps. This material will serve as a road map for the Trial Chamber, in order to have a brief understanding of what it is the Prosecution will seek to prove in this case. Rather than simply explaining to you what happened, we will endeavour to show you what happened by way of contemporaneous material, including, as I indicated, documents. This opening will focus on documents. First, some brief information about the accused in this case. A former professional soldier in the Yugoslav People's Army, Rasim Delic attended the Command Staff School of the JNA between 1988 and 1999, and he requested to leave the JNA on the 13th of April 1992, as the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina began. Shortly thereafter, he was involved as the head of training and operations organ of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he later headed the Vozuca tactical group, before becoming a member of the Main Staff of the Territorial Defence, with responsibilities for organising and commanding armed combat activities in a number of municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In October 1992, he was appointed the acting head of the Department for Operations, Planning, and Training in the Main Staff of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On 8 June 1993, the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina restructured the Army Supreme Command headquarters to include establishing the post of Commander of the Main Staff, the position to which the accused was appointed to fulfill. The document which has been marked as PT-11-86, which Your Honours will be -- or will be placed before Your Honours during the course of this trial, is a document of the 8th of June, 1992, signed by the President of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic. This is the decision on the redistribution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Supreme Command headquarters and the appointment of senior officers. Paragraph 1 of this document establishes the post of Commander of the Main Staff of the armed forces, while at the same time retaining the staff or the position of Chief of the Main Staff. Paragraph 4 of this document indicates Rasim Delic shall be appointed Commander of the Main Staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is paragraph 4. If we then look at paragraph 6 of the same document, it indicates that persons appointed under paragraph 4, such as the accused, Rasim Delic, are hereby relieved of the posts they have hitherto held. The Prosecution submits that this paragraph is important in understanding the overall document, because we would assert that based on this document, and the fact that Rasim Delic was relieved of his prior responsibilities, is a clear indicia that as of the 8th of June, he assumed the new position as the Supreme Commander. Again, 8 June 1993, signed by Alija Izetbegovic, President of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency. Let me turn now to the issue of the Mujahedin. This case -- you will hear in this case exclusive evidence and extensive evidence as to the involvement in these crimes of the Mujahedin. These people who were foreign fighters, who began entering Bosnia in 1992, joined a number of units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the period 1992/1993, before being formed in August 1993, as we'll explain in a few moments, in the El Mujahedin Detachment. With respect to the arrival of the Mujahedin, a witness you will hear tomorrow, a journalist by the name of Andrew Hogg, went into Bosnia in the summer of 1992 with the explicit aim of seeking to find some of these foreign fighters and interview them. He worked at that time for "The Times of London." Andrew Hogg was able to locate and identify a leader of these foreign fighters; a man by the name of Abu Abdel Aziz. He then interviewed this individual in August of 1992. That interview was tape-recorded, and you will hear that interview tomorrow in full. Prior to this interview, it's important to point out that Abu Abdel Aziz required the permission of the Bosnian authorities before he granted Mr. Hogg the interview, and Andrew Hogg obtained this permission, from, as we will expect he will testify, the army Command post by the waterfall in Travnik, and the interview was conducted. Just a few words about Abu Abdel Aziz. This foreign fighter, who is from Saudi Arabia, was alternately known as Barbaros or Red Beard. Mr. Hogg, we expect, will testify that some of these foreign fighters, including Abu Abdel Aziz, as you see in the photograph, would put henna in their beard in order to dye it, so that they would look appropriate upon being martyred before Allah. That is what Mr. Hogg will testify about why Abu Abdel Aziz has coloured his beard in this way. This individual was relatively well known in the Jihad community. He had fought in Africa, Kashmir, the Philippines, and Afghanistan, and he was in central Bosnia by the summer of 1992, and, again, was the subject of the interview which you'll hear tomorrow. In effect, Abdel Aziz was the first commander of these foreign fighters in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, among some of the questions which Mr. Hogg addressed to Abdel Aziz, in the summer of 1992, was the issue of why did Mujahedin come to Bosnia; and if everything goes to according to plan, we'll hear a little clip from that interview to explain why the Mujahedin came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The next question that might be of importance is: Where did the Mujahedin come from? And, again, with respect to that question, Abdel Aziz provided the following answers to Mr. Hogg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Abdel Aziz was also asked by Mr. Hogg about the level or type of support which these foreign fighters received from the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the summer of 1992, and here is what Mr. Aziz had to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With respect to the issue of command and control over these foreign fighters in the summer of 1992, Abdel Aziz had the following to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's interesting, in that clip, Mr. Abdel Aziz made reference to the Muslim forces; and although the transcript said "inaudible," I believe, and when you hear this tomorrow, if you listen carefully, you can hear him say, "Muslimanske Snage." I'll talk about the Muslim forces or the Muslimanske Snage in a few moments. But I think it's important to understand and realise at this point exactly what it is Mr. Abdel Aziz is talking about when he talks about Muslim forces, and so I highlight that at this point so that when we talk about that in a few moments, you can link that back up with what Abdel Aziz had to say. The final clip from this interview I'd like to share with you at this point is simply where were the Mujahedin active in this time period, the summer of 1992, when Mr. Hogg interviewed Abdel Aziz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to now turn and briefly put before the Trial Chamber some photos and some basic information about other leaders of the foreign Mujahedin; that is, the foreign fighters who came to Bosnia. A number of witnesses throughout this trial will be talking about such individuals, and so I think it's important at this point to simply start thinking in terms of linking photos and images of these people so that we understand who they are. The first person is an individual by the name of Sheikh Anwar Shabbah. Shabbah, an Egyptian, was the dominant spiritual leader within what ultimately became the El Mujahedin Detachment. You'll see a number references in today's opening and throughout this trial to the EMD, that's the El Mujahed Detachment, a unit which was formed and was within the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 3rd Corps, in 1993. Sheikh Anwar Shabbah was killed in December 1995, shortly after the conclusion of the Dayton Agreements. The next leader is known widely as Abu Haris. Abu Haris, again, was a senior commander of the El Mujahedin Detachment. He replaced a individual by the name of Vahudin, as the commander of the Mujahedin in late 1992. An Algerian, Abu el-Maali, or Abu Maali, traveled to Bosnia in 1992. He replaced Abu Harith Alibi as emir of the El Mujahedin Detachment,; that is, as leader of the El Mujahedin Detachment. His headquarters, which we'll also be hearing about throughout this trial, the abandoned Vatrustalna factory complex in Zenica. Zenica, of course, being the location where the ARBiH, the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 3rd Corps headquarters was located. So, again, you'll hear numerous references in this case to Zenica, which was the location of the Army's 3rd Corps. Muataz, this individual is an Egyptian, a veteran of the Afghan war, was responsible primarily for training. He ran the training centres that the EMD and the Mujahedin ran and was the chief of military operations and training, beginning in late 1993, following the death of Vahudin. In August of 1994, he was officially promoted to the rank of captain in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; and in 1995, he was killed in a series of clashes with the VRS, the Army of the Republika Srpska, near Vozuca. Next, Vahudin, you've heard me refer to him a couple of time already, an Egyptian. He also was involved in the war in Afghanistan, against the Soviet Union, and was responsible, among other things, for prisoner exchanges, and particularly, a well-known prisoner exchange in Zenica. He was killed in the autumn of 1993, when there was fighting between the ABiH, or ARBiH, and the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, in central Bosnia-Herzegovina. Aiman Awad, a Syrian, also known as Abu Aiman, studied medicine in Zagreb, prior to the war, and consequently was fluent in the B/C/S language, as we now call it. He was tasked, among other things, translating documents and maintaining contacts with other leaders within the ARBiH. Due to his language skills, he was at various times personal aide and liaison to Abu el-Maali; and similar to several of the other person we've talked about, was promoted to the rank of captain in the to Army of the Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina in August 1994. And, finally, Abu Hamza. Similarly, Abu Hamza had studied medicine in the former Yugoslavia, spoke the language, and was a senior leader within the El Mujahedin Detachment in 1994-1995. These individuals will be referred to throughout the course of this trial, and, again, we thought it might be helpful at this stage to briefly introduce you to these individuals. Let's talk now about these foreign fighters in the period from the summer of 1992 until August of 1993, when the El Mujahedin Detachment was formed; that is, these foreign fighters in that year-long period before the formation of the El Mujahedin Detachment. At this point, let me just make a few comments about what Abdel Aziz referred to as the Muslim forces or the Muslimanske Snage. We'll see numerous documents where the reference that included the abbreviation "MS" for Muslimanske Snage. Similarly, the Muslim armed forces or the Muslimanske Oruzane Snage, or MOS. These were early units that the Prosecution submits were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry for that. Were these words used interchangeably to mean one and the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, they were, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that intervention. The MS or the MOS were used interchangeably, and these were early units that the Prosecution will lead evidence on concerning how members went from various units of the ARBiH. And we'll see some documents and some material about that during this opening and throughout the course of the trial. Let's take a look now at what's been marked as PT6001. This is a video clip of an oath-taking ceremony in the Central Bosnia-Herzegovina town of Travnik on 21 August 1992; and if you look carefully, you will see Abdel Aziz speaking to these assembled troops at this oath-taking ceremony outside the madrasa in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What you see here, Your Honours, is the mufti of Travnik, Mufti Abdubegovic [phoen], translating the comments of Abdel Aziz from Arabic into B/C/S for the benefit of the soldiers who were present. Unfortunately, the quality of the tape is not very good in terms of the audio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the script.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the video. The building in the background is the madrasa in Travnik. The individual in the center of the screen with a beard is a man by the name of Makteuf. His name may also come up during the course of this trial, although not particularly extensively. Makteuf is an Iraqi who was in that unit. Let's take a look now at a list of the Travnik Muslim forces. This is PT1014. Again, what we're going to do a number of these documents is show you snippets or excerpts from a number documents that highlight certain aspects of the Prosecution case. This document, dated the 15th of September, 1992, indicates a list of soldiers from the Travnik area. And, again, what we've done here is placed the B/C/S and the English texts on the same slide. This is a list of soldiers in the Muslim forces or the Muslimanske Snage in Travnik. If you again look, this list, which again there will be a number of these lists that show how soldiers moved from one unit to the other, including into the El Mujahedin Detachment, this document contains the list of the names of the first nine persons on this list, and you see there number 2 is Mr. Makteuf, the individual I just pointed out to you in the videotape, as well as a number of other individuals, some of whom will feature in this case. This document was signed by the commander of that unit who -- Mr. Redzic. The next document, similarly, is a list. This one from the Defence Staff of the Territorial Defence of the Travnik. And, again, you will see a number of individuals, some of whom were also on the previous list. And in the far right-hand column in the handwritten of the script, it's not so legible in this page, but it will be in the next, it says "Muslimanske Snage." And these are the individuals, including as you see on this page of this document a number of who you will see on this document, a number of individuals who do not appear to have names that would come from the former Yugoslav. These are some of the foreign fighters who are in the Muslimanske Snage. All of these documents, we believe, will be in evidence during the course of the trial and will allow the Trial Chamber to make its own conclusions with respect to these foreigners in units, including the Muslimanske Snage or the MOS. Let's talk a little bit about foreign fighters in the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. And, again, this will be some of the circumstantial evidence that the Prosecution will lead with respect to the presence of foreigners in that unit. PT1043. Now, this is a document, dated 15 March 1993, that indicates the combat disposition and engagement of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. The report indicates that at that point in time, mid-March 1993, the brigade had 1.439 men divided into three battalions. The 1st Battalion of the 7th numbered around 325 soldiers and was engaged in Bijelo Bucje and in Ravno Rostovo. The 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, it continues in this paragraph, indicates men in Gornji Vakuf, men in Vitez, men in Visoko. And at the end, interestingly enough, it says additionally, there are around 60 Arabs and Turks, who are also not included in this total which might sound a bit strange in terms of the wording, but this is part of the evidence that the Prosecution asserts shows that there were, at this point, in time in mid-March 1993, 60 Arabs and Turks within the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. This document was signed for the Commander of that brigade by Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The signature --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The signature on this document is that of Mr. Amir Kubura, who was signing for the Commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see, Asim Koricic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's a good point, Your Honour. If you see to the immediate left, where it says "Komandant," you'll see handwriting. It is actually the letters "ZA," meaning "4." So Asim Koricic, at this point in time, was the Commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. He must not have present on the 15th of March, and Amir Kubura signed on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The next document, PT1055, a document dated the 2nd of April, 1993, is addressed, you'll see, at the bottom. And it's indicated that it's a warning, and it's addressed to the HVO command of the Central Bosnian operation zone to Mr. Dario Kordic. In this document, the Commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade issues a warning to Mr. Kordic. Kordic, at this point in time, was a commander of the HVO, as counterpart unit within the HVO, the Bosnian-Croat Defence Council. And in this, the Commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade is complaining about incidents of arrest, harassment, abuse, or even killing of members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade by members of the HVO units. And he goes on to state: "The saddest part is that this is also being done to foreign nationals, volunteers in our ranks, particularly those from Arab countries. We warn you, Mr. Kordic, to release all foreign nationals, both members of the BH Army and civilians." This is a theme that you will see in a few of other documents that we'll be showing you in just a couple a minutes. These are complaints by the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, a unit of the 3rd Corps of army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, complaining to the HVO units about harassment of Arabs, foreigners, volunteers, members of our units. This, again, we would submit, is evidence that within the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, there were such foreign citizens. The next document, PT1056, is a bulletin, dated the 4th of April, 1993, from the Security Administration of the Staff of the Supreme Command of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And in this document, which again is a Security Administration document, a bulletin, if you will, which is addressed to, among others, the Main Staff of the armed forces: "Members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade --" This is a complaint about a check-point incident in Travnik. Members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade were inside the car. The driver was a citizen of Bosnia, while the rest of them were from Arab countries. And at gunpoint, they were harassed by members of the HVO at this check-point. The next day, the military police of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade found one of the foreign citizens who had been so heavily beaten up that he's probably died by now. They go on to report that a corpse of a male found between 30 and 35 was found in the zone of responsibility of the 306th Mountain Brigade, again, a unit of the 3rd Corps of the ARBiH. We have reliable information that he was a foreign citizen and most probably a member of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade; again, the ARBiH Security Administration on foreigners who were killed by the HVO at check-points. The next document, PT1059, 12 April 1993, a report of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade on "Members of our Brigade taken prisoner by HVO members." This document is signed by Ahmet Adilovic, the assistant commander for morale, information and propaganda, and religious matters within the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. He goes on to report an increasing number of HVO cases where members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, again, have been stopped at check-points, taking prisoner foreign citizens who are members of the BH Army, i.e., "volunteers who are in unit." He goes on to query why the HVO would do that because the foreigners are only fighting against the Chetniks. In other words, why would the Bosnian Croats harm or attack our foreign nationals in our units. They're here to help us in our joint fight against the Serbs." This document goes on to list a number of individuals who have been taken prisoner by the HVO, including five Arabs and two Iranians who were taken to the barracks in Kajenik [phoen], which is an HVO location. We see names and countries of origin including Pakistan, Algeria, Tunisia, and Egypt. They go on to talk about three Arabs and three Iranians or Turks who are in prison in Kiseljak, again held by the HVO. And it goes on to talk about two other individuals who were killed at a hairpin bend near Novi Travnik and others taken prisoner at that location as well. And finally an indication of three Saudi Arabians who were arrested near Vitez and are probably now in Kajenik and again in the hands of the HVO and three turks and two or three Arabs who were imprisoned, again complaints by the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade about mistreatment of its foreign soldiers, its Mujahedin soldiers. Let's turn now very quickly to PT1102, which is the minutes of a 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade meeting on the 18th of May, 1993. And the subject of this meeting, interestingly, is the distribution of war booty. One of the members attending this meeting complained about the lack of organisation in collecting booty stemmed from their lack of experience, that unit, the 7th, lack of experience in distributing war booty and indicates that the Arabs did not permit access to one ammunition explosives depot. It goes on to issue the conclusions from this meeting, that Afandi Adilovic who we saw earlier talking about the HVO mistreatment of the foreign citizens, is charged with holding talks with the Arabs about the war booty which they took. Let's turn now to Bijelo Bucje. We indicated earlier that that was one of the locations where the first battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was active, and again June 1993 we see an order delivered to the 3rd corps command, the subject this is responsibility for not obeying orders, this document again signed by Amir Kubura on behalf of the commander or for the commander Asim Koricic. Paragraph 2 of this document indicates the Commander of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, that's MBBR, immediately sent a unit of 70 soldiers to the Bijelo Bucje sector. "Counter-attack was carried out from three directions. During the action, four soldiers, foreign citizens, Arabs, were killed." Again, demonstrating the presence of these foreign fighters within the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in the period prior to the formation of the El Mujahedin Detachment. Let's move to the 306th Mountain Brigade. This is another unit within the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina that the Prosecution has alleged contained some foreign fighters. Now, the school in Mehurici. Mehurici is a small village. It's located near Maline and Bikosi, you'll hear a lot of evidence about events in Mehurici, you'll hear evidence about the school Mehurici. This was known as the headquarters for the Mehurici Arabs, if you will, or the Mujahedin until they moved out of this school to a location at Poljanice, several hundred metres away from the school just outside the actual border, if you will, of the small town of Mehurici. Forces of the 306th Mountain Brigade were also in the school headquartered in the school at the same time the Mehurici Arabs were there before they relocated to Poljanice. This document, dated the 25th June, 1993, is a report, a handwritten report on the state of combat morale in the units in the area of responsibility of the 306th Mountain Brigade. This document indicates that a lack of coordination between the units, again, in the 306th Mountain Brigade area of responsibility, lack of coordination between the units, the 306th, the 17th, the 312th, the 314th, the 7th, Arabs from Mehurici, and MS, mostly Muslimanske Snage from Mehurici, led to the situation that several soldiers died; in other words, there was a lack of coordination between these various units within the 306th Mountain Brigade's area of responsibility, and it makes reference to the Mehurici and the MS, Muslimanske Snage, from Mehurici. This document was signed by the Assistant Commander of the 306th Mountain Brigade for morale, information, and propaganda, and religious affairs, Halil Husic, and we'll see his name also come up in other documents in a few moments. So a little bit about Mujahedin in other units; that is, foreign fighters in units other than the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade and the 306th Mountain Brigade. The next document dated the 16th of June, 1993, which is addressed to the 3rd Corps Command and to the Commander personally states: "Since the beginning of the war, volunteers from foreign countries and a group of Bosnians united in a so-called guerrilla unit, have been staying on the territory of Zenica." Again, 3rd Corps headquarters: "With the aim of their focused engagement in our struggle I hereby order send these groups to Igman and merge them with the Supreme Command Staff independent detachment in Zukic unit, otherwise they should have hospitality withdrawn and possibly disarmed." This document is signed on the 16th of June, 1993, by the accused, Rasim Delic. El Jihad or Brigada Jihad. There came a time in 1993, prior immediately prior to the formation of the El Mujahedin Detachment in August, that the foreigners began coalescing into a unit which they called "El Jihad" or "Brigada Jihad" this name became relatively well-known throughout the area, and as we'll see in just a moment, official documents of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina began referring to this unit as "Brigada Jihad" or"Jihad Brigade." Let's take a look at PT1433. This is a document of the 306th Mountain Brigade dated 30th of July, 1993, addressed to the 3rd corps sector for morale guidance, information and propaganda, and in religious affairs, and in this document you'll see a reference for different motives and number of combatants has joined the newly-formed El Jihad Unit, where they train, are not on the front line, are financially stimulated, et cetera. Again, the 306th Mountain Brigade is making reference to the newly-formed El Jihad Unit, 30 July 1993, again signed Halil Husic, who was the assistant commander for morale guidance, information and propaganda and religious affairs of the 306th Mountain Brigade. The next document, PT1454, 10 August 1993, we're moving much closer to the formation of the El Mujahedin Detachment, a report to the President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on changes in the battlefield for 9 August 1993: "Discontent is growing amongst the soldiers in the zone of responsibility of the Bosanska Krupa operations group after a company from the 1st Brigade of the 17th Glorious Mountain Brigade abandoned its position on 8th August and returned to the camp with the intention of joining up with the El Jihad Unit." Again, 10 August 1993, signed by the accused, Rasim Delic. Let's turn now to the El Mujahedin Detachment itself. A brief explanation on some of these military documents that you'll see. This document is, I believe, the first document that was sent by way of an electronic communications system that was used by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina known by the name "Packet" or "Packet communications." You see the line all the way across this document. Above that line, basically, is the information that indicates when the document was received. So this document was received on 13 August 1993 at 10.03 in the morning. Below that line, you'll see information about when the document was sent and who sent it. This document was sent from Zenica on the 12th of August, 1993. This is a proposal. This is a proposal for the formation of a detachment of foreign citizens, dated 12 August 1993, received in Sarajevo on 13 August 1993. It's addressed to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina armed forces Supreme Command Staff. And in this document, or in this request, which was sent, as we'll see in a moment, by Enver Hadzihasanovic, who was the 3rd Corps commander and who later became the Chief of Staff to the accused Rasim Delic, this proposal was for the formation of a unit with all foreign volunteers in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Army in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps into a detachment. In other words, put all of the foreign volunteers into one unit. Mobilisation collection point for the detachment, Mehurici. The name of the unit, El Mujahedin, its number -- military unit number to be determined by the Supreme Command Staff, logistic support coming from the 3rd Corps. "We request urgency," says Commander Hadzihasanovic. Thirteen August 1993, the same day the document is actually received in Sarajevo, we have an order for the formation of the El Mujahedin Detachment in the 3rd Corps zone of responsibility. This document is addressed to the 3rd Corps command and is signed again by Rasim Delic. In this order, he indicates that the creation of the El Mujahedin Detachment is to begin immediately and to be finished no later than 31 August 1993. The newly-formed unit shall be registered under the 3rd Corps. And he directs that the appointment of officers shall be done according to regulations. Shortly thereafter, a ceremony was held where the El Mujahed Detachment, in effect, was formally established. The following video clip shows this formation ceremony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Shortly thereafter, or as early as 16 August 1993, 3rd Corps Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic issues an instruction to the Commander of the Operation Group Bosna indicating that 50 members of the El Mujahedin Detachment are interested in going to the front line at Zavidovici. Now, you'll recall the 13 August 1993 order dictated that the El Mujahedin Detachment be formed no later than 31 August 1993, yet here three days after that order we already see the 3rd corps commander referring to the El Mujahedin Detachment, leading to the presumption that the unit was formed relatively quickly after the 13th August 1993 order, because the 3rd corps commander, which was the overall command under which the El Mujahedin Detachment functioned, is already indicating that 50 soldiers of this unit were interested in going to the front lines at Zavidovici and indicating that if the Operation Group Bosna commander could provide transportation or fuel, that those soldiers would be made available to him. The next document is again one of the number of lists which the Prosecution will put before the Trial Chamber during the course of this trial. This one, again the copy is not particularly high quality, but in the upper left-hand corner you'll see "Republika BiH," Republika of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 3rd Corps, El Mujahedin Detachment," this is a list of soldiers in that unit. Unfortunately, it's not dated, but it does indicate with a serial number of 001/93. And in this document, which contains the first and last names, place of birth and a column indicating, in the ABiH sense, we can get or begin to get a sense of who some of these persons were that were early members of the El Mujahedin Detachment. And I've provided in this visual that's now on the screen several excerpts from this document. I'm not going to highlight any names in particular, but I will indicate to the Trial Chamber that a number of the witnesses that we will be calling, particularly in the next few weeks, name appear on the excerpt that was just visible on the screen, and those witnesses will be talking about the early formation of that unit. Similarly, towards the end of the document we begin to see -- and again this is early -- this is 1993, early in the period of the EMD, the El Mujahedin Detachment. We see Pakistanis, an Englishman, a Palestinian, a Dane, a Moroccan, Kenyans, Jordanians, Saudi Arabians and persons from Qatar. This document also contains an overview of El Mujahedin Detachment in the sense of the detachment command staff. And who do we see listed at the Emir or commander - that's a term that was used within the El Mujahedin Detachment, the Emir - Dr. Abu Haris, whom we met a few moments ago. "Deputy" -- and this is a quote from the document: "Deputy," that is, the representative of the Emir in Zenica, Abu Maali, Military Commander Wahiuddeen, et cetera, Deputy of the Military Commander representative in Zenica, Muataz. At the bottom, Deputy Commander for Security, Abu Iaman. With respect to command and control over the Mujahedin in 1993, this document, which is a document sent by a field worker from the UN Centre for Human Rights, reports -- and this is October 1993, interestingly enough, October 1993, several months after the El Mujahedin Detachment is formed. Meeting -- reports on a meeting with the Deputy Commander of the 3rd corps of the BH Army, Dzemal Merdan, this was a meeting in 23 September and answering the field officer writes -- answering my question concerning the Mujahedin factor he - that is 3rd Corps Deputy Commander Dzemal Merdan - explained that there are no Mujahedin units in the BiH Army. That's untrue. But there are many volunteers from a number of countries, including some Westerners, they came to fight back modern fascism, and all of them are required to obey orders and to respect the laws of the army." We would submit that this is one of several instances where the -- even the presence or the formation of the El Mujahedin unit was something which leaders of the 3rd Corps and other units within the ARBiH denied. Let's turn finally to PT2880. We're fast-forwarding now towards the end or past the end of the El Mujahedin Detachment. 26 February 1996, this document is instructive for a couple of purposes. First of all, again, it's a list of members of the El Mujahedin Detachment. You see clearly the VJ number. That's the military unit number that we saw referred to earlier, where a military unit number would be assigned. The Mujahedin Detachment was 5689. Any document or reference to 5689, VJ5689, is the El Mujahedin Detachment of the 3rd Corps of the Army of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a list of all the members of that unit. And, again, it starts off with Saudi Arabians, Turks, Algerians, Palestinians, Libyans, Tunisians, South Africans, et cetera. If we go to the very end of this document, above the signature line of Sakib Mahmuljin, who was the 3rd Corps Commander during the period of 1994-1995, you'll see that this list contains 1.774 names on it. And towards the end of this list, which you see above the signature block, you see a number of individuals who clearly are from Bosnia-Herzegovina, Travnik, Gornji Vakuf, Sarajevo, Zenica. Let's turn now to the crime base. Maline-Bikosi, 8 June 1993, the very day which the Prosecution submits Rasim Delic was appointed the Commander of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the 5th of June, 1993, three days prior to the alleged crimes, we see a report and a proposal. This is a document from the Operation Group at Bosanska Krajina, a unit of the 3rd Corps of the ARBiH, which included the 306th Mountain Brigade. Let me briefly explain what we have here is a number of corps, military corps, the 3rd Corps being the prominent one in this case. Under the corps, there were a number of operational groups which were established, some of them for longer periods of time than others. The operational groups then consisted of brigades,, so that we have Corps, Operation Groups, Brigades, and then of course Battalions, Companies, Platoons. The operation group, Bosanska Krajina, at this time period, June 1993, included the 306th Mountain Brigade. For purposes of what we're going to be discussing right now, that's important to understand. This is a proposal, dated the 5th of June 1993, to the 3rd Corps commander from, from the OG Bosanska Krajina commander. He's ordering the commander of the 306th Mountain Brigade to organise a unit on the strength of one battalion to move on the axis of villages of Maline, Radonjici, Krpeljici, Velika Bukovica. And towards the little church, the little chapel, Sveta Ivan, with the aim of deblocking Travnik. The next document, a telegram, or at least written on a telegram form, from 306th Mountain Brigade to 3rd Corps Command. Time of recording, 8 June, 2210 hours. And what do we have? The 306th Mountain Brigade commander reporting: "We are currently on the line Maline, Guca Gora, Mosor, Velika Bukovica, exactly in conformity with the plan of the OG Bosanska Krajina commander three days earlier." The next document, again, from the 306th Mountain Brigade, to the 3rd Corps, dated 9th June, indicates the presence of that unit having taken Maline. "Our forces," towards the bottom: "Our forces reached the line of villages Maline, Guca Gora, Mosor, Velika Bukovica yesterday." That would be on the 8th of June. And in a regular combat report to the Supreme Command Staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated 9 June, again, we see a report that: "Our forces have taken or are on the line along Maline, Prcanj, Dzumalija [phoen] and requesting additional support for those units." The 306th Mountain Brigade was the unit which we will assert or do submit, which had foreign fighters in it, went into Maline on the 8th of June, 1993. On the morning of 8 June 1993, approximately 200 to 300 people, including Bosnian Croat civilians and HVO, that is, Bosnian Croatian Defence Council, that's the Bosnian Croat Army, let's make sure that we're all clear on that. The HVO is the Bosnian Croat army. Approximately, two or 300 people, including Bosnian Croat civilians and HVO members from the villages of Maline, Podstinje, Podovi, and Matici had gathered in Gornji Maline, when Maline was taken by the ARBiH on the morning of 8 June 1993. A very brief lesson in the B/C/S language. "Gornji" as a prefix means "Upper." You will hear some of the translations, where the witness is being translated, it will come across as "Upper Maline." "Donje" means "Lower." So in this instance, what we have here, the village of Maline having in effect two parts: Upper Maline and Lower Maline. Following negotiations on that morning, these 200 to 300 Bosnian Croats, who were in Gornji Maline, surrendered to the ARBiH forces at about 1100 hours in the morning. The HVO members surrendered their weapons, and some of the witnesses will talk about the presence of Mujahedin in the village while the Bosnian Croats were surrendering or shortly thereafter. The 200 to 300 surrendered HVO members and Croat civilians were then ordered to form lines with the intention that they would walk from Gornji Maline via Bikosi, which is over a relatively steep mountain, towards Mehurici. They were escorted by armed ARBiH soldiers. As the column left Gornji Maline, the men and women were separated. Those who had been wounded during the attack were left behind in Gornji Maline. The main group of Croats - or at this point I'm talking about the men - the main group of the men, including the surrendered HVO members and the Bosnian Croat civilian men, was led by the ARBiH, via Bikosi, down to Poljanice, which is where the Mujahedin camp was located after having left the school in Mehurici that we saw before. And in this map, you can clearly see Mehurici in the upper right. Right below the letter "H," you see the abbreviation "SK." That's the school on this map. That is the school. Right below that, the "L" shape below "SK," is the school in Mehurici. You also see the word "Poljanice." That's the Mujahedin camp, and we've marked that on this map, the Mujahedin camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At this point, are you able to tell us how many were these who managed to go forward of the captured people?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Of the captured people, there were -- there were more than 200 people in this line, moving from Gornji Maline up to Bikosi and then down towards Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The number 200 to 300 relates to the number after the women were separated and the wounded were left behind?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The number 200 to 300 refers to the total start group. After the women are taken out and the wounded are left behind, there are still approximately 200 people in this column. So there are 200 men, approximately, moving in this direction in these columns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As this group or this column approaches the camp, the Mujahedin camp in Poljanice, approximately nine Mujahedin, five locals and four foreigners, all carrying automatic weapons, came out of the Poljanice camp. We believe the evidence will show that the locals who had joined with the Mujahedin were wearing masks in order to hide their identity; whereas, the foreign Mujahedin felt no need to conceal their identity because the local people would not know who they were. They stopped this column. These nine Mujahedin stopped the column. They held the ARBiH commander, who was escorting them, and the military police commander at gunpoint; and at that point made a further separation of this group, taking approximately 30 to 40 of the males out of the column and, in effect, ordering them to turn around and head back towards Bikosi. The remaining group - that is, as you see on this slide - the main group continued to the school in Mehurici; 30 or 40 taken out of the group, ordered to turn around, head back; the remaining people head towards the school in Mehurici. On the way back towards Bikosi, the Mujahedin line up the captured Bosnian Croat men in front of trenches and threaten to kill them. That does not happen at this point, however. Meanwhile, back in Gornji Maline, the group of the wounded Bosnian Croats that had been left behind were put on a truck or trucks by the soldiers, the ARBiH soldiers, together with the Mujahedin who boarded at least one of the trucks with an automatic rifle. This truck is then driven towards Bikosi. But before getting there, it stops and the wounded are ordered to get off the truck and begin walking towards the camp in Poljanice or towards Mehurici, just as the other group had done from Bikosi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to give us the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Of the wounded? No, it's a bit unclear. There were certainly than a handful of people, but I can't be much more specific than that. Now, at this point, what we now have is a situation where the 30 to 40 men are returning back from Poljanice back towards Bikosi, when they encounter this group of wounded walking down the mountains towards Mehurici or towards Poljanice and Mehurici, as you see on the slide before you. At the point the two groups meet, the wounded group is now ordered to turn around and join the group of 30 to 40 people marching or walking back up towards Bikosi. And this is, again, on an upward trajectory. You have Maline on one side, Mehurici on a low side, Bikosi on one a mountain in between the two, if you can envision that. So we now have a situation where the wounded, plus the 30 or 40 captured Bosnian Croat males, are walking back in the direction of Bikosi. Shortly before the group reaches Bikosi, the only woman in the group, Ana Pranjes, was shot dead by one of the Mujahedin soldiers. And after this murder, the group continues walking up hill, where they reach a junction, the decision was taken to go towards Bikosi, rather than on the way around the mountain back towards Maline. At this point, as this group is at or about this junction, perhaps a little bit farther up - it's not a very far distance from the junction to the few houses that constituted the village of Bikosi - Sreco Bobas, one of the captured HVO soldiers, suffered an epileptic seizure. Now, the witnesses that you hear on this count will testify about of him having a fit. A couple of the witnesses knew him and knew that he suffered from epilepsy. So for them, it wasn't anything completely unexpected. They knew him, he was a neighbour, and they knew he suffered from epilepsy. Sreco Bobas had an epileptic seizure at this point in time. The Mujahedin began firing indiscriminately at the entire group of Bosnian Croat men at this point. The Mujahedin then continued firing at close range with single shots, we would submit, to kill off any of the survivors, until one of their own soldiers apparently was accidentally shot during this gunfire, at which point they withdrew. As a result, 24 Bosnian Croats were murdered. Agreed Fact 39 provides their identity. The Defence have agreed that these 24 people were, in fact, killed that day at Bikosi. Of course, the issue as to how and who, and who had effective control, is in dispute. But the fact of the matter is the parties have agreed that these 24 people were murdered on the 8th of June, 1993, in and around Bikosi. The survivors, there were at least six people who survived this massacre. Several of them suffered serious gunshot wounds, but otherwise survived. Briefly, among the survivors: Zeljko Puselja, shot in the right arm; Darko Puselja, wounded in the left shoulder and the left side of his ribs; Marian Bobas, in his right shoulder; Berislav Marijanovic wounds to his legs; Zdravko Pranjes superficial wounds in the chest and leg; and Pavo Barac, who escaped with miraculously with only scratches. Marian Bobas and Darko and Zeljko Puselja were later captured by the ARBiH and detained in the Mehurici elementary school gym until 4 July, when they were transferred to the KP Dom Zenica, the Zenica music school, or otherwise released. Now, why do I mention that? Why do I mention that? As we'll see later, when the opportunity comes to investigate exactly what happened at Bikosi on the 8th June 1993, it's certainly relevant that there were survivors of that shooting incident who were being detained by a unit of the ARBiH, affording the opportunity to properly investigate what happened, because the survivors, or at least three of them, were in the custody of a unit of the ARBiH. That's one of the reasons why it's particularly relevant with respect to the survivors and what happened to them in the immediate aftermath of this massacre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is meant by "otherwise released"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there were a number of instances where combatants were exchanged, prisoner exchanges, prisoner of war exchanges, et cetera. So I believe that at least one of these individuals was the subject of a prisoner exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit about notice of the crimes committed in Bikosi. On the 13th of June, 1993, Enver Hadzihasanovic sends a report directly to the accused, Rasim Delic; and in this document, he makes reference to foreign fighters, volunteers from foreign countries, Arabs and Turks. He makes reference to the so-called guerrilla group, and we saw an earlier document signed by the accused making reference to the guerrilla group. They were in this territory even before the formation of the 3rd Corps. In fighting to date, they have been acting outside the usual context and lawful methods of combat, which is directly detrimental to the BH state. Now, in complete transparency, Hadzihasanovic does not make reference to the events in Maline or to Bikosi in this document of the 13th of June, but he does make reference to acting outside the usual context and lawful methods of combat. Two days later, 15 June, in a document addressed to the commander of Main Staff of the BH Army, personally; again, that's the accused, Rasim Delic. A document indicating that, again, serious crimes are being committed in the area of the 3rd Corps; Susanj, Ovnak, lack of coordination murders are getting away. One of the reasons these people are leaving, these are Bosnian Croat areas. This document is referring to crimes being committed in the area of an area around Zenica. This is the first of several documents coming from Stjepan Siber, the deputy commander of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And let me here just stop to again, brief information for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. The accused, Rasim Delic, Bosnian Muslim, overall Commander of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, two deputies, a Bosnian Serb by the name of Divjak and a Bosnian Croat deputy, Stjepan Siber. Stjepan Siber, in this document here, is raising complaints about crimes committed by the ARBiH against Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Croat areas. We'll see, in just a moment, additional documents where General Siber raises further complaints about what happened in Maline. 23 June 1993, a document he addresses to the Commander of the 3rd Corps, Hadzihasanovic, and the chief of the Security Services Centre, Mr. Asim Fazlic. Siber informed us in his document, or this is actually a document of General Delic and Mr. Bakir Alispahic, who was the Minister of the Interior. Siber informed us in his document about "serious security problems in your area," and this is addressed to 3rd Corps commander and this addressed to the civilian police chief, if you will. The facts indicate that increasing number of members of the armed forces are among the perpetrators of the most serious crimes. So Delic and Alispahic are sending this document to their respective military and police commanders concerning crimes in the area of Zenica. 24 June, in a document addressed to the Supreme Command Staff and, for your information, to the President of the Presidency, we have a document that indicates, in the village of Mehurici, 247 civilians are placed in the gym of a school. That would include at this point the women, wounded, all those people who made it to the gym at Mehurici: "They are under the protection of the 306th Brigade," the Mountain Brigade we talked about before. "They are also subject to a lethal danger from the so-called 'Death Brigade,' composed primarily of Mujahedin foreigners billeted in the immediate vicinity." 25 June, another document where, again, General Siber, referring to earlier notice documents he sent, he asks -- he takes the liberty to insist to the President of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, and the Army Supreme Command Staff Commander, Rasim Delic, he assists on them coming to Zenica to sort out the problems with respect to foreigners.
