PT1328 also goes on to say: "On 8 June, 1993, 35 Croats were executed in the village of Bikosi. Four witness were wounded, but survived. Personal changes in the 3rd Corps command are essential." This is the Deputy Commander of the ARBiH warning General Delic and putting him under strict notice, as of the 25th of June, that 35 people have been murdered in Bikosi. One or two more documents on this. Again, 3 July, approximately a week later, again to the BH Army General Staff Commander: "Please reply to my letter of 3 July. I, again, request and insist that you, the BH President and the BH Mini Minister of the Interior, come to this town before it is too late. I do not have the power or competence to make any major changes without you." Signed Stjepan Siber, Deputy Commander. It's not until the 17th of October, 1993, after President Izetbegovic receives a letter from the special rapporteur, Tatuous Masovetski [phoen], about crimes in Maline, that Rasim Delic finally takes steps. And on the 17th of October, Rasim Delic orders the 3rd Corps command to look into allegations of a massacre of 25 Bosnian Croats, and it says in parenthesis "civilians" in village of Maline he requests necessary information, including the name of the units that participated; a short account of the combat situation; whether the massacre was occurred, and if so, what was the extent; if there was a massacre, the measures taken against the perpetrators. He gets a report back several days later from Mr. Asim Delalic [phoen], who was the security officer of the 306th Mountain Brigade; and in this document, Asim Delalic reports: "Please note all persons were killed during the combat activities." And that information then is reported, notwithstanding the fact that his deputy commander had warned him about massacres, that information is reported to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, so they can respond to Mr. Masovetski's request, this international special rapporteur's request, and they explain that it was combat fatalities. "It can be seen from the above that in this case the massacre which is being attributed to the RBiH Army did not take place. As a result of an armed conflict caused by extremist HVO forces, 25 people were killed on one side, including villagers of Croatian nationality," signed by the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? We started at five past 4.00. I'm not quite sure, at this stage, how long we can go for before we go on a break. Let's find out from the recorders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm advised the interpreters would like a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We always listen to the interpreters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What time shall we come back, at 6.00? Court will adjourn and come back at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, may the Trial Chamber just apologise to you for not asking you whether it was a convenient moment to take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That was actually a fine moment, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's move on, then, to the next issue concerning the incident or the massacre at Bikosi, the issue of whether the perpetrators of this crime were ever actually punished. Document PT2918 is a letter that was received by the Office of the Prosecutor from the Cantonal Public Prosecutors Office in Travnik, dated the 16th of April, 2002, in response to some queries our office made concerning whether this event was investigated and prosecuted. According to this document, they report that the District Military Court and the District Military Prosecutor's Office in Travnik and the Travnik District Military Court and District Military -- Prosecutor's Office in Vitez were functioning during between January 1993 March 1994 and according to the information that was available to that office and the archives which that office accessed in order to assist the Office of the Prosecutor, there was no documentation relating to alleged war crimes committed by members of the BH Army, other than for a few crimes in question which do not relate to the incident in Bikosi. We'll lead extensive evidence on this failure to punish these perpetrators. Similarly, we sent a submission to the Zenica Cantonal Court and Zenica and Travnik are neighbouring municipalities, and because the location was -- is very close to the Zenica Municipality, we actually asked both municipalities, in the event that the case may have been improperly before a court at that point in time and again the Zenica District Military Court or the Zenica Cantonal Court reported that there were three cases involving war crimes during the relevant time period and not a single case was tried in the period in question with regard to members of the ARBiH; that is, not a single soldier of the BH Army was prosecuted for war crimes during a relevant time period in the Zenica Cantonal or, at that point in time, Zenica District Military Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do they say who was involved in the three war crime cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, they do, and we can get you that document. That letter will contain that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Finally, then again in 2006, we made further inquiries with the Cantonal Court in Zenica, and this is PT2946. And in response to that, they wrote back to us, indicating that regarding existence or non-existence of other files or documents "Please be advised that no trials were conducted --" Or they actually say, "No reports were received, no trials conducted, nor any indictments were submitted for the murder of 25 Croatian civilians on 8 June 1993 in the area of the villages Maline and Bikosi." Again, extensive evidence will be led with respect to this failure to punish concerning the crimes in Maline. Let me turn now to 1994. There are no crimes alleged in this indictment concerning 1994. However, we will lead evidence to show that throughout that time period, the Mujahedin were again involved in criminal activities which the accused was put on notice for. This evidence, we submit, goes to the issue of his knowledge as to the propensity of members of the El Mujahedin Detachment to commit crimes, and therefore it is relevant for that limited purpose of knowledge and notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that evidence going to be very detailed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, it will not be detailed at all, Your Honours, and it's primarily documentary evidence. But of course we may require one or two witnesses to explain these documents and the steps taken particularly with respect to what I'll be describing in a few moments, an operation known as Operation Vranduk, but we don't expect to lead extensive evidence on that, but simply some evidence to demonstrate that notwithstanding the fact that there were no crimes charged during this time period, members of this unit continued committing crimes, and the accused was aware of those crimes, which goes, in our submission, to the point of the propensity of members of that unit to commit crimes and the knowledge of the accused thereof. 1994 January, the murder of Paul Goodale. Paul Goodale was a humanitarian worker who was in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we will see from this document, PT1679, that on the 29th of January, 1994, an operative plan was put into effect in order to determine the circumstances under which Mr. Goodale was killed. Three UNHCR workers, Simon King, David Kurt and Paul Goodale were kidnapped on the 27th of January, 1994, by unidentified uniformed persons with beards and dark complexions, according to this document. Later, around 2130 hours that evening, Paul Goodale was shot and murdered. This document calls for "in view" -- as it says: "In view of the security assessment, the following operative measures shall be put into effect: Make an assessment of the persons of interest to security, referring to members of the El Mujahedin Unit, and the related persons and forward it to the Ministry of Defence Security Sector." The document goes on to indicate that on based on the information then available, it was likely that members of the El Mujahedin Unit were involved. Such persons needed to be interviewed, and they warned, in effect, that there would likely be a less-than-positive reaction on behalf of the El Mujahedin Unit to this investigation. PT1783, August 1994, again a document relating to the El Mujahedin Detachment. In this document, it indicates: "With the formation of the units involving the foreigners, there was a great influx of foreign citizens from Afro-Asian countries." I should also warn Your Honours that in a number of these documents of the ABiH, there are a references to persons from"A/A" countries and many of the people in Bosnia-Herzegovina refer to foreigners as persons from African or Asian countries, and so sometimes we'll see the abbreviation "A/A" or persons from "A/A" countries, and those are the same thing, in our submission, the Mujahedin, the foreign fighters, persons who came from North Africa or the Middle East, if you will. There's a great influx from foreign citizens from Afro-Asian countries, the channels to which they came to the ABiH, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were mainly through the Republic of Croatia. The final destination was Central Bosnia, where in the beginning they joined the existing ARBiH units, and after a certain period of time several units were formed whose members were mainly foreigners of Afro-Asian origin as well as Bosniaks; that is, Muslims. Problems with these foreigners started immediately after their arrival in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it then begins to list some of the problems that they had, such as the difficulties with the locals, provoking the locals, attempts to introduce a particular brand of Islam Vahabism, which is Saudi-based form of Islam, et cetera. And then this document continues: "One of the most serious incidents," it reports, "was caused by members of this unit happened on 27 January 1994 when Paul Goodale was killed. The main suspect, Abdul Hadi el-Katani [phoen] was abducted by four masked men during his transfer to Sarajevo." And then it goes on to report: "Various incidents whose perpetrators are members of this detachment occur daily." This are just examples of their scandalous behaviour, that is, behaviour which disregards laws of this state, and he goes on. This is signed by General Sakib Mahmuljin, ARBiH 3rd Corps Commander in August of 1994. As a result of this, and as a result of these continued crimes in the 1994 period, what came to be known as "PO Vranduk, or "Preparatory Process Vranduk," was undertaken. And this is was a situation they were going to place the El Mujahedin Detachment under surveillance for a number of reasons, and we'll talk about those in just a moment. But beginning in 1994, at the latest, Preparation Process Vranduk was underway, which led to this Operation Vranduk being ordered into existence in 1995. PT2069 relates to this, and we see "OA-Subject: Operation Vranduk" concerning the El Mujahedin Detachment, the 3rd corps, and their contacts. I will again be quite frank with the Trial Chamber. There were a number of reasons why Operation Vranduk was put in place. The alleged criminality of the El Mujahedin Detachment was by no means the sole motivation for placing this unit under surveillance. We'll see that in the documents. But at the same time, there are references in this documents to the criminality of members of that unit as being one of the reason why Operation Vranduk was put in place. The document goes on, and it's, again, a Security Administration document that we are looking at: "The El Mujahedin Detachment is by its formation an organisation and entity comprised of a number of African-Asian nationals whose behaviour is very suggestive, from a security point of view." It goes on: "Apart from the aforementioned and a number of illegal activities and actions committed by some members of the detachment, there is also a significant issue of evading participation in combat activities. Brigadier General Jusef Jusarovic [phoen], who was the head of the Security Administration, therefore, suggests," or he indicates "'with the aim of monitoring, documenting, and intercepting intelligence activities and shedding light on all activities of the members of this detachment.'" He suggests the introduction of operative action in the El Mujahedin Detachment. At the bottom of this document, the accused, Rasim Delic, approves the commencement of Operation Vranduk. Among the other reasons, as I indicated, in addition to the crimes, there were some indications that members of the El Mujahedin Detachment were reporting information to outside intelligence agencies of outside states and/or were reporting what was happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina to outside states. That's why the Security Administration was heavily involved in this Operation Vranduk as well. So we are asserting that there were two reasons: These outside intelligence activities of the El Mujahedin Detachment and this alleged criminality. But regardless of the actual reason for the establishment of Vranduk, as we will see, by placing the El Mujahedin Detachment under surveillance in 1995, the accused was being informed on a regular basis about the activities of that unit, including alleged criminality. And we will lead evidence to that effect during the course of this trial. Let's go to the next document. This is a report, 15 June 1995, information report, concerning the El Mujahedin and intelligence, and it reports right at the outset members of the El Mujahedin Unit continue to conduct reconnaissance: "In the past ten days or so, members of the unit destroyed several dugouts, liquidated tens of Chetniks, instilled panic and fear. Following the killing of a member of the El Mujahedin Unit, they organised a squad of combatants who barged through defence lines, liquidated a number of Chetniks, slaughtered two, and carried their heads through the villages down the Krivija [phoen] River, showing them to the locals and the school children." On the front line, soldiers are receiving food and fruit from them, the El Mujahedin Unit, as well as ammunition and other necessary things, and saying they would not want the unit to leave their AOR; that is, other ARBiH units did not want the Mujahedin Detachment to leave: "We will continue to follow the conduct of El Mujahedin Unit members through operative work in the field and subsequently report to you." And will you see, during the course of this trial, a number of such reports concerning the activities of the El Mujahedin Detachment. Let's turn now to the Kamenica Camp, the focus of a number of the crimes in the 1995 crime base. In April 1995, as indicated on PT2016, the 35th Division Command. And now let me again explain briefly to the Trial Chamber what's gone on here in terms of the difference between the 1993 crime base and the 1995 crime base. I told you earlier this afternoon that in 1993, below the corps level, there were what were called operational groups. By 1995, the concept of the operational group was replaced with the more western or NATO terminology of a "division." So divisions were implemented; and by 1995, below the corps level, we have divisions which consisted or were made of the battalions rather than operations groups. So what we have here is a document from the 35th Division Command to the 3rd Corps, copied as well to the El Mujahedin Detachment. And in this document, April 1995, we see, under paragraphs 5, 6, and 7, the 35th Division is indicating that a deployment area for the El Mujahedin Detachment should be made -- should be prepared at the 12th kilometre. And, again, this is a location where the Kamenica Camp eventually was built. It refers to the 12th kilometre point south of Zavidovici on the highway or on the road. Sometimes it's referred to as 12 kilometres, sometimes it's referred to as 13 kilometres. As we've explained in the indictment and in our Pre-Trial Brief, it's all the same thing. Whether they talk about 12-kilometre camp or 13-kilometre camp or Kamenica Camp and, it's all the same thing. And in this document, we see that this location, the 35th Division of the 3rd Corps, is making this location available for the El Mujahedin Detachment, to be used, as they put it, their deployment area. Now, what was in this location? Well, at the location where the camp was built, there were about two houses which were abandoned. There was a red building and another building that didn't have a roof. There was a number of tents were established, as we saw in one of the earlier photos, including a tent that was used for prayers. And there was also an area that many of the witnesses referred to as the football field. Now, it's unclear whether it was actually marked out as a football field. It was simply a big, grassy area where they often played football, and they refer to that. You'll hear the witness refer to that as the football field. Throughout its existence, this camp was operated by the El Mujahedin Detachment of the 3rd Corps of the ARBiH. Turning to the military operations in 1995. Again, unlike the situation in 1993, where the crime base was as a result of an armed conflict or combat between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO, that is, the Bosnian Croats, the situation in 1995 involves combat between the ARBiH and the VRS, or the Bosnian Serb army, the army of Republika Srpska. What we have in 1993 are Croat victims. What we have in 1995 are Serb victims, and the conflict in 1995 is the conflict between the ARBiH and the VRS. Now, between April and November of 1995, the ARBiH, 3rd Corps, 35th Division, which at this stage included the El Mujahedin Detachment, conducted four operations, the primary purpose of which was to liberate the territory in the Vozuca pocket area. These are four combat operations at various points in time: In April 1995, we have the Operation Behar 95; in May, Operation Sabur 95; in June-July, Operation Proljece 95. Proljece meaning "spring," as in the season; and between 10 September and 10 October 1995, Operation Farz, which is also referred to in a number of documents as F-95. These are the four military campaigns during this time period that all relate to liberating this territory from the Bosnian Serb Army. Operations Behar 95 and Sabur 95 were not as successful as the Main Staff would have hoped, which was why Operation Proljece 95 was put into place. The strategic objective was to gain the Ozren salient and the foothill areas around Vozuca and to liberate that territory from the VRS. The Mujahedin Detachment was involved in this operation. During the course of the trial, there will be some evidence about the planning of this operation and how it was set forth, simply to give the Trial Chamber enough understanding and background to show that the El Mujahedin Detachment was actively involved both in Proljece 95 and Farz 95. Again, not a lot of evidence will be led on this. This is not an unlawful attack or an unlawful conduct of hostilities case, but it is important to understand the background of these military operations to show, again, notice that the accused was aware that the El Mujahedin Detachment was participating in these combat operations and also goes to the issue of the prisoners that were actually taken during that -- those combat operations. Again, the actual operational maps of Proljece 95, signed off by Favil Hasanovic, who was the 35th Division commander. And you will see in this document, along the front lines is marked -- or the proposed lines of attack, as marked, you will see "EL-M," indicating the location where the El Mujahedin Detachment was to be involved in this operation. PT2075, as early as 15 May 1995, a plan of attack is being proposed or put forward. And this document, signed by Abu Maali of the El Mujahedin Detachment, indicates: "We have planned an attack on the Podujevo sector on three axes," indicating what the El Mujahedin Detachment is planning with respect to this operation. PT2130, again, sets forth an analysis of the attack and how it's proposed to go forward, and regular combat reports then went forward, including on the 6th of July, 1995, as this operation is underway. A report to the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina indicates that the El Mujahedin visited the 35th Division command in order to coordinate tasks for the upcoming operations; again, indicating that the accused was on notice that the El Mujahedin Detachment was going to be involved in this operation. Finally, on 16 July 1995, with respect to Operation Proljece, we see an order undertaking active combat operations, addressed to a number of corps, including the 3rd Corps: "Immediately undertake active combat operations on the entire front along selected areas." On the 18th of July, the following day, a report on the progress to the Main Staff command post in Kakanj, indicates that pursuant to the orders of the Supreme Command Staff, the combat is underway and units of the 35th Division in coordinated action with the El Mujahedin Detachment carried out the necessary preparations, and "we expect the beginning of the attack shortly. The detachment command will set the time of readiness, since El Mujahedin is the main unit in charge of the coming assignment." The July 1995 crime base. In the early hours of 21 July 1995, the El Mujahedin Detachment of the 3rd Corps launched an attack in Krcevine in the Zavidovici Municipality. Soldiers of the VRS were captured and taken to Livade, a village not too far away. During the evening of 21 July 1995, soldiers of the El Mujahedin Detachment could be heard shouting "Allahu Akbar," and then an El Mujahedin soldier entered the room where these prisoners were being detained, carrying the severed heads of two of the prisoners of war: Momir Mitrovic and Predrad Knezevic. While detained in this building in Livade for two or three days, these captured VRS prisoners were subjected to daily beatings before being taken on the 23rd of July, 1995 to the Kamenica Camp. That evening, upon arrival there, the prisoners were blindfolded and taken to the football field, where a number of them were beaten and otherwise mistreated. The following morning, Gojko Vujicic was shot and killed in the camp. The soldier -- the El Mujahedin Detachment soldier who killed Gojko Vujicic then retrieved a sabre from the prayer tent, decapitated the corpse, and the prisoners of war were then forced to kiss the severed head, which was then hung from a wall on the cell where they were being detained. The following day, the mistreatment continued to include beating with objects such as rubber hoses. At least one prisoner was threatened and wounded by a foreign member of the El Mujahedin Detachment with a sabre. The prisoners were taken outside and high-pressure air hoses were tied around their legs, resulting in severe pain. On the afternoon of 23 or 24 August, the prisoners were brought to the football field and, again, severely beaten and electrical shocks were inflicted upon them from batteries. On the 28th of July, 1995, a report on the action of the El Mujahedin Detachment was sent to the General Staff of the Army Military Security Service Administration; and in this report, it's indicated that a reliable source had reported on the El Mujahedin activities. And it indicates in this document that ten to 15 captives were being hemmed in, and further reports that the El Mujahedin Detachment will continue to be monitored. And the information was completely reliable and the source was accurate. We point out, we believe, evidence will be established that during the time period while these prisoners were being kept in the Kamenica Camp, the accused, Rasim Delic, visited the 35th Division command post in Zavidovici, approximately 12 kilometres from the camp, with President Izetbegovic and the 3rd Corps commander, Sakib Mahmuljin. The basis for that is PT2356, which indicates, in a regular daily combat report of the 35th Division, that one of the factors having a positive impact on combat morale was, in fact, the visit of the President of the Presidency, the Chief of the Main Staff, the accused, and the Commander of the 3rd Corps. On the 24th of August, 1995, these prisoners of war were transferred to the KP Dom Zenica, which is a civilian prison. KP Dom is a correctional penitentiary in Zenica, where these prisoners were held for a few more days until they were finally exchanged and released. The ARBiH security Main Staff Security Administration was informed of these developments as well, and these prisoners were interviewed and interrogated while at KP Dom Zenica. And, again, this goes, we would submit, to the issue of whether those prisoners were debriefed and/or interviewed with an eye towards criminal prosecutions with respect to those persons who committed the crimes in that camp during that time period. 30 August 1995, in a briefing for the Chief of the Military Security Service Department of the 3rd Corps, again, a further report on intelligence activities concerning persons from African-Asian countries. And we have further information about the efforts being taken. And this document is important because it indicates that the security organ of the 35th Division has noted all these incidents, not specifically relating to the camp but relating to other activities, and this is why this is important. But they did not take energetic measures, as they did not want to disrupt relations with this unit, meaning the El Mujahedin Detachment, so as to ensure successful completion of combat actions. "We don't want to intervene because we don't want to disrupt combat operations that would involve the El Mujahedin Detachment." Let's turn now to Operation Farz or F-95. Unlike what we've been talking about thus far, Operation Farz, this operation lay along the fault line, if you will, between two corps of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Operation Farz, at this point, what we have is the 2nd Corps coming from the north and the northeast, and we have the 3rd Corps towards the southwest on this front. The 2nd Corps' code name for this joint operation was "Uragon" [phoen]. So you'll see some documents relating to Uragon. Uragon and Farz were complimentary actions that were designed to squeeze the Bosnian Serbs in the Vozuca area, in this Ozren saline of the Vozuca pocket. So you'll see some references in some of the documents to Uragon. That's the ARBIH 2nd Corps counterpart, if you will, to F-95 or Farz 95. This operation took place in September of 1995. And, again, as early as the end of August, we begin to see the planning process for this operation, and we see an order from the accused, directed to the commanders of the 2nd and 3rd Army, or Corps, if you will, to carry out preparations and draft documents for the liberation of the Vozuca pocket. And that document is, again, under the signature of the accused, which leads us to Operation Farz. The map you see before you is, in effect, the planning map for Operation Farz. You'll be able to see a larger version of this, and it indicates clearly that it's designed to go from 10 September to 10 October 1995. On the 28th of August, 1995, in preparation for this operation, we see that the commands of the 3rd, 4th, and 5th Battalions of the 329th Brigade are to set forth the conditions for training of their troops in the organisation of the El Mujahedin Detachment; that is, the El Mujahedin Detachment is now being charged for training three battalions of the 329th Mountain Brigade in anticipation of this attack. The 3rd Corps logbook, which has an "F" indicated for, again, the date period starting 26 August, the "F" we would submit relates to" Farz." On 2 September 1995, and, again, these are excerpts from this logbook, indicates at 2000 hours the Commander of Subordinated Units briefed the 3rd Corps Commander: "From 1000 to 1800 hours today, the commander of the of the 37th Division, the head of the Tesanj, Teslic, and Doboj municipalities toured an El Mujahedin Detachment. On 3 September, we see orders concerning F-95 to the command of the 328th Brigade, an El Mujahedin Detachment, to pull out 55 Mujahedin members of the Asim Camdzic Company and to re-subordinate them. What this shows, Your Honours, is a very clearly-defined level of involvement of the 3rd Corps and 35th Division commanders redeploying the El Mujahedin Unit, or subcomponents the El Mujahedin Detachment, throughout the active combat operations, or in the preparatory stages of that combat operations, clearly showing that this unit was a full-fledged component unit of the ARBiH, 3rd Corps, and particularly the 35th Division. This is not just some rogue soldiers who are just roaming around somewhere on the battlefield. We have clearly defined orders, re-subordination, requests for training, et cetera. Similarly, PT2513, 3 September 1995, fortification of combat positions pursuant to a demonstrated need and as requested by the El Mujahedin Detachment, and in order to provide fire support, "I hereby order the fortification of combat positions for antiaircraft guns," et cetera. We see fortification orders at the request are being undertaken at the request of the El Mujahedin Detachment. 7 September, supplement to order for attack, addressed to the 3rd Manoeuvre Battalion, El Mujahedin Detachment, and commands. Here we see an order directing that the 3rd Manoeuvre Battalion command is to join the El Mujahedin Detachment command for the execution of the task as requested by the El Mujahedin Detachment command. So we see re-subordination of units to the commander of the El Mujahedin Detachment. The document goes on and indicates that the 3rd Manoeuvre Battalion commander will be at the El Mujahedin Detachment forward command post, from where they will jointly conduct command and control. Another logbook, PT2561, and the relevant time periods, 9 September 1995, that is, on the eve of the commencement of Operation Farz: "2015, the commander of the 35th Division informed the commander of the 3rd Corps that everything was going according to plan. Forty-five minutes later, the commander of the El Mujahedin Detachment and Aiman Detachments had a meeting with the 3rd Corps commander at the 3rd Corps IKM forward command post." Let's return to that Operation Farz map that we looked at a little bit earlier. Again, the time period, 10 September to 10 October. On the upper left-hand corner of the map, "Approval, General Rasim Delic." Delic has approved this Operation Farz map as put forward. Let's return to the logbook, PT2465. This is the 3rd Corps, Operation Farz, 26 August, the starting day of this. Under 10 September 1995, at 0620 hours, and this is Day 1, Operation Farz. At 0620 hours, El Mujahedin Detachment informed the 3rd Corps commander that the specific task was almost complete, i.e., that Paljenik was mopped up in less than five minutes: "Following this initial success of our forces, everything transpired with lightning speed. From one minute to the next, the Chetnik strongholds fell one after the other." "By 1000 hours, Our forces succeeded in expelling the Chetniks from a number of locations, where our forces were able to join up at the very entrance to Stog village." The logbook goes on to report: "These exceptional results and military victories in dominant facilities in the general sector of Vozuca were achieved by the joint units of the 3rd Corps, i.e., the El Mujahedin Detachment; the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th Manoeuvre Battalion, which were the units that had been subordinated; Garrison Units of the 329th and 328th. By the 11th of September, the following day, we have new assignments being reflected in the logbook, the new axis of attack in the zone of responsibility of the 35th Division, El Mujahedin Detachment, and the 2nd Manoeuvre Detachment are attacking and taking a number of additional locations. Now, an interesting point. At the time Operation Farz is being launched, the accused, Rasim Delic, is not in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, after his return, he's interviewed by a journalist in Sarajevo. And she asked him about this operation and the fact that he was outside of the country at the time this operation was being undertaken. Here's what he had to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, we would submit that what the accused told this reporter - and particularly at the beginning of this exchange, was particularly important in this context - he says: "One must know that these operations had been planned for a long time, and I personally watched over every one of those maps; that they began on 9 September, that is, the day after I left for Malaysia, but they kept being performed under my immediate supervision because the system of command and control functions, although one is not physically present at the site, because I was in continuous contact and secured that all that keeps functioning." Immediate aftermath of Operation Farz, and then we'll turn to the September 1995 crime base. On 11 September 1995, while the accused is in Malaysia at this conference, the 3rd Corps logbook reports that the President of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, will come for an inspection tour of the unit "tomorrow"; and, in fact, the logbook on the 12th indicates that President Izetbegovic did, in fact, make such a visit to these locations. Let's turn now to the September 1995 crime base. On 11 September 1995, the 2nd Company of the 5th Battalion of the 328th Mountain Brigade, while undertaking Operation Farz, captured approximately 60 people, primarily Bosnian Serb army soldiers, but a few civilians, including three females who had remained after Vozuca was taken. The soldiers, along with a few women and children, surrendered in groups in the upper part of Kesten, near a creek. They surrendered to the 2nd Company of the 5th Battalion of the 328th. One such group of Serbs was captured in the forest in the afternoon by ARBiH soldiers, which included some members of the El Mujahedin Detachment. They were then taken to the village of Kesten. On the road, on the way to Kesten, Zivinko Tadorovic and Milenko Stanic were killed by soldiers of the El Mujahedin Detachment, and they never actually made it to the village of Kesten. Soldiers of the El Mujahedin Detachment then immediately took away four other Bosnian Serb Army prisoners of war who have never been heard from since. The remaining group of prisoners, including a few civilians and the women, are then taken to a hall in Kesten. Shortly thereafter, the three women are taken away to another location, which they themselves were not sure where it was. Shortly after that, additional members of the El Mujahedin Detachment arrive and take charge of the Bosnian Serb Army prisoners of war who had been in the custody of the 5th Battalion of the 328th Mountain Brigade. PT2596, a regular daily combat report, makes reference -- this is a 328th Mountain Brigade combat report of 13 September, and this document reports on 11 September two companies of the 5th Battalion captured 61 hostiles and three Serbian women. Members of the El Mujahed Unit took charge of all captives except two, while the two were turned over to the 328th Brigade military police. Now, PT2596 makes reference to the capture of 61 hostiles and three women. PT2575 is a contemporaneous list of the detainees that was compiled by a member of the 5th Battalion of the 328th Mountain Brigade at Kesten. This document refers to a total of 62 persons. Let's take a look at 2356, a list of the detainees or the persons -- this list was made in Kesten. And if you look at this document, it has a numerical sequence up to 51, followed by an explanation: Four taken by Arabs immediately; three women, one was set free, two killed on the road to Kesten, two children released; altogether, 62. Now, these numbers don't quite exactly add up. I will tell you that the 51 persons listed on this document, their names and identities are all set forth in an annex to the indictment. There's one person who we submit was not included on this list, and we are unable to explain how that happened. But the bottom line is, Your Honours, we would submit that these numbers are certainly close enough that in a combat situation or shortly thereafter, that one person might be -- one person's name might not show up on the list, and that's not something that is particularly fatal under these conditions to the Prosecution's case. But I do draw that to your attention, because there is a discrepancy in the numbers. The 51 named individuals are listed in the indictment along with one other individual who we have evidence to suggest was with this group, but for whatever reason his name was not included on this list that was made at the Kesten hall. Returning to 11 September 1995, the soldiers of the EMD thereafter took these prisoners of war from the Kesten hall to the Kamenica Camp. Shortly thereafter, the women, who had been taken to an intermediate location, are also taken to the camp, where they're placed in a wooden shed, or "wooden structure," as they describe it, on the grounds of the Kamenica Camp. In the period from 11 to 17 September 1995, the male prisoners of war were subjected to cruel treatment. The women heard screams and shouting and the sounds of beatings and gunfire. On three or four occasions, military commands to the effect of, "Prepare your weapons and shoot," were heard, followed by bursts of gunfire, and we believe the evidence will show that some of the victims were mutilated with a saw or other type of cutting device during this period in early mid-September 1995. The three women were detained in the Kamenica Camp for several days, during which time they were mistreated. They were then transferred on the 13th of September, 1995, to the Vatrostalna building in the village of Brezik on the outskirts of Zenica, which was the headquarters of the El Mujahedin Detachment. These women were kept in that location for approximately two weeks before they were also transferred to the KP Dom Zenica, where they remained until they were released. They remained there about six weeks before they were released on the 15th of November, 1995. But let's return to the Kamenica Camp and the 52 captured VRS soldiers who had been taken prisoners of war on 11 September. During this time period, in addition to the beatings and other mistreatment I mentioned a moment ago, a number of these men were shot. Some were murdered in other ways, including decapitation. Each of these men that was murdered was murdered in and around the Kamenica Camp. By 17 September, fewer than a dozen of the original group of 52 captured on the 11th of September were still alive. PT2964, a document which we believe will come into evidence, is an exhumation report concerning an exhumation at a riverbank near the Kamenica Camp, where several of the corpses of these persons that were captured on the 11th of September and subsequently taken to Kamenica Camp, where their bodies were located. On the 17th of September, 1995, a further group of approximately ten VRS soldiers surrendered to the ARBiH a few kilometres northwest of Vozuca on the main road between Vozuca and Zavidovici. This group was initially taken to a building in Brezik, Zavidovici Municipality, that was then occupied by soldiers of the El Mujahedin Detachment. After being briefly detained there, this group of soldiers was similarly taken to the Kamenica Camp. During the time period these soldiers were detained in that camp, they were interrogated, similarly beaten with sticks and rubber hose, and otherwise mistreated by soldiers of the EMD; and, again, electrical shocks were administered to them, and one of the prisoners was threatened by an EMD soldier with having his ear cut off. At the time this group of ten soldiers arrived on the 17th, as we've indicated a few moments ago, there were still a few survivors from the group of 52; and on the 18th of September, seven of the surviving 52 group from the 11th were taken out onto a field, where gunshots were then heard, and none of those seven men were ever seen or heard from again. Sometime between the 20th and 22nd of September, 1995 - and we pin that date on the fact that it was a couple of days or a few days after the 17 September group arrives - Nenad Jovanovic, an elderly Bosnian Serb man, who was detained in the room with the group of ten from the 17th of September, was beaten, stripped, and given water mixed with petrol to drink. He died a few days later in the camp. On the 29th of September, the group that was captured on the 17th of September is transferred by the ABiH or ARBiH 3rd Corps military police from the Kamenica Camp to the KP Dom Zenica. So we have the group of ten that was captured on the 17th remaining in the camp until the 29th, at which point they are transferred to KP Dom Zenica. By the time they leave on the 29th of September, 1995, three or four of the remaining group of 52 from the 11 September capture are still alive in the Kamenica Camp. Those three or four prisoners of war who are from that group of 52 have never been heard or seen ever since. Now, briefly I'm cognizant of the time, Your Honours, I will not be able to finish today, but I do have one last area I do need to focus on, and then I think I need another half hour tomorrow to complete. With respect to notice, we believe that the totality of the notice evidence that will be led, from the beginning, from Day 1 of his assumption of command as the ARBiH Supreme Commander, that Rasim Delic was on notice that members of the El Mujahedin Detachment had a propensity to commit crimes, and that these crimes were particularly directed non-Muslims, such as what happened in Maline, when foreigners were involved that eventually ended up being members of the El Mujahedin Detachment; to the crimes in 1994; to the notice that he received from Operation Vranduk; and into the July 1995 crime base. The accused was certainly on notice that members of this unit, in particular, were extremely dangerous and had a propensity to commit crimes, and under no circumstances should there have ever been a situation where this unit was put in charge of prisoners of war. Let me briefly touch on the issue of whether anyone was investigated or punished for the crimes in Livade, Kesten, or the Kamenica Camp in the period from July through September 1995. There will be evidence led that no soldier of any ARBiH unit was prosecuted or investigated for these crimes. Again, documents were sent, requests were made to the relevant military prosecutor's office and military courts and the archives that currently hold those collections, to look through this material. And the final document I want to share with you, PT2943, a letter from October 2006, addressed to the Office of the Prosecutor, whereby we had asked for, again, official confirmation for them to go back into the archives and search for any information that might suggest that anyone was investigated or prosecuted for these crimes. And we see, in paragraph 2, the chief prosecutor of the Zenica-Doboj Cantonal Prosecution Office which holds these archives, there were no files or other documents which would indicate that the following was carried out: Submission of criminal reports, investigation or pressing of charges related to the following events: Number 1, Maline, and we've already talked about that; number 2, murder and maltreatment of three prisoners of war in the village of Livade; murder and maltreatment of 62 prisoners of war, members of the VRS, in the area of Kesten. And they make reference to the lists of names of victims which was provided to them with respect to these crimes. We would submit, Your Honours, that no one has been brought to justice for any of the crimes that we've alleged in this indictment, and that failure to punish these perpetrators rests with this accused, Rasim Delic. As I've indicated, I believe I need approximately 30 minutes to complete this opening tomorrow. We will then call the first witness. I, again, do not anticipate that his evidence will take us past tomorrow. The witness scheduled for Wednesday will be available to testify on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Does that bring us to the end of your presentation for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For today, I think, Your Honour, in light of the time. I think in 30 minutes tomorrow, perhaps a little bit less, I'll be done with the opening, and we'll call the first witness in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. Due to the lateness of the hour, court adjourns until tomorrow at 2.15 p.m. in Courtroom II. Court adjourns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 10th day of July, 2007, at 2:15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
